color-analysis.summary: Matching clothing and makeup colours to your skin undertone, hair and eyes so the shades near your face flatter you and your complexion looks brighter.

quick.overview:
Color analysis assigns you a palette, traditionally one of four seasons (spring, summer, autumn, winter), based on your skin undertone, hair and eye colour. The payoff people want is a clearer, brighter-looking complexion and a more harmonious face, simply from wearing the colours that sit best next to it.

The chain is direct: colours worn near the face reflect onto skin and change how it reads, so the right shade can make skin look healthier and the wrong one can make it look sallow. The method was popularised in the early 1980s and went viral on TikTok in the early 2020s. Studies have found people prefer clothing hues that harmonise with their skin tone, while the specific season categories have little peer-reviewed validation.
quick.how: Practitioners hold coloured fabric near the face, usually in daylight, and judge how it affects skin, eyes and contrast. Results are then turned into a palette for tops, scarves, makeup and hair colour. Variants expand the four seasons into twelve or more sub-seasons by adding undertone, lightness and chroma. The effect of a colour is visible immediately, so many people simply test shades in a mirror.
quick.risks: There is no physical risk. Costs come from paid consultations and from buying new clothes to fit a palette. Different analysts and apps can assign the same person to different seasons, and early systems were criticised for centring white clients.

angle.text: You get sorted into a palette based on skin undertone, hair and eyes, then wear those colours and makeup shades near your face so your complexion looks brighter and healthier. The effect of a colour shows up the moment you hold it up. Studies show people prefer clothing hues that harmonise with their skin tone.

voice-maxxing.summary: Training pitch, resonance and delivery to sound deeper, more masculine or more confident, using techniques borrowed from speech therapy.

quick.overview:
Voice maxxing is the practice of changing how you sound, most often aiming for a deeper, more resonant voice that comes across as more attractive and authoritative. Looksmax.org has long-running threads on how much a deep voice adds to attractiveness and how to get one.

The chain runs through habits rather than anatomy: pitch is set largely by vocal fold length and tension, with typical adult male speech around 90 to 155 Hz and female around 165 to 255 Hz, and therapy works on breathing, resonance and pitch habits. Speech-language pathologists use these methods for voice disorders and gender-voice care; no published trial has tested them as an attractiveness intervention.
quick.how: People work on breath support, relaxed resonant speech, lower habitual pitch and pacing, often with a speech-language pathologist or with recordings of their own voice. Practice is gradual and builds over weeks of regular speaking habits.
quick.risks: Training taught by a clinician is low risk. Forcing the pitch lower can strain the voice, and therapy sources stress vocal hygiene. Surgical or hormonal changes to the voice are separate medical topics.

angle.text: You practise pitch, resonance and delivery techniques, borrowed from speech therapy, to sound deeper or more masculine and come across as more attractive and confident. The change builds through trained habits in how you breathe and speak. Speech-therapy methods exist for voice change; they have been studied for medical and gender-voice care.

dripmaxxing-fashion.summary: Upgrading clothing, fit, accessories and styling to look sharper and more put-together without changing your face or body.

quick.overview:
Dripmaxxing means improving how you look through clothes, fit and accessories rather than surgery or products. "Drip" is hip-hop slang for stylish dress. The payoff is a sharper, more put-together look and, proponents say, higher perceived attractiveness, visible as soon as you are dressed.

The chain is direct: well-fitted clothes flatter body proportions and shape first impressions. Forum users call it one of the easiest and most reversible changes. Research on how clothing affects the wearer (enclothed cognition) has had mixed replication results, and no clinical trials exist on dripmaxxing itself.
quick.how: People work on fit first (tailoring, sizing for shoulders and length), then colour, simple outfit formulas, shoes and accessories. Many pair it with a haircut and grooming changes. Results show right away, and a basic wardrobe can be built gradually.
quick.risks: There are no medical risks. The main caveat is cost, particularly where hype brands and resale markets are involved; spending on them is optional.

angle.text: You improve clothing, fit, accessories and styling to look better without changing your face or body, and the difference shows as soon as you are dressed. Good fit flatters your proportions and sharpens first impressions. It is a low-cost approach discussed widely in forums.

beard-maxxing.summary: Growing and shaping facial hair to frame the jaw, disguise a recessed chin and add a more masculine lower face.

quick.overview:
Beard maxxing means growing, trimming or enhancing facial hair to change how the lower face looks. The appearance payoff is a framed jaw, a stronger-looking chin and added masculinity; forum users call it one of the cheapest and most visible looksmaxes and discuss styles for different jaw shapes.

The chain is direct: a beard adds a hair outline to the jaw and chin, which changes how the lower face reads. Beard growth is driven by androgens such as DHT and by genetics. Research cited by Wikipedia suggests bearded faces are rated as more dominant, while findings on attractiveness are mixed.
quick.how: Most people grow the beard out over weeks, then shape the neckline and cheek line and keep it trimmed to suit their jaw. For sparse or patchy growth, topical minoxidil (studied in one placebo-controlled trial) and beard hair transplants are discussed. The change is visible as the beard fills in.
quick.risks: Grooming carries minor risks such as ingrown hairs; pseudofolliculitis barbae is a documented shaving-related condition. Beard transplants are surgery with the usual procedural risks.

angle.text: You grow and shape a beard to frame the jaw, disguise a recessed chin or add masculinity, and the change shows as the beard fills in. Minoxidil or transplants are sometimes used for patchy growth. Research on how beards affect attractiveness has produced mixed results.

squintmaxxing.summary: Habitually narrowing the eyelids slightly to get an intense "hunter eyes" look; free, instant and reversible.

quick.overview:
Squintmaxxing means slightly narrowing the eyelids, in photos and in daily habit, to get the look called hunter eyes: a lower upper-lid line and a more intense, less wide-open gaze. It costs nothing and can be stopped at any time.

The chain is mechanical: narrowing the lids lowers the visible upper eyelid line and reduces the amount of eye shown, which proponents say changes the impression of the eye area. It is promoted on looksmax.org; no studies have tested whether it changes perceived attractiveness.
quick.how: People practise a small, relaxed narrowing in the mirror and in photos, aiming for a controlled look rather than a strained squint. The effect is visible immediately and is usually combined with other eye-area changes such as brows and posture.
quick.risks: Squinting is generally regarded as harmless; an ophthalmologist quoted on Wikipedia cites temporary headache from muscle tension as the only harm. Forum claims about wrinkles or temple balding have no published support.

angle.text: You narrow the eyelids slightly, in photos and in daily habit, to get the intense look called hunter eyes. It is a free, instant adjustment that lowers the upper-lid line. Its effect on how others rate your looks has not been studied.

dental-work-teeth-maxxing.summary: Whitening and tidying teeth with strips, pastes and dentist treatments, often alongside orthodontics, for a brighter, neater smile.

quick.overview:
Teeth maxxing means improving how teeth look, mostly by whitening them with strips, pastes, trays or dentist treatments, often alongside orthodontics and other dental work. The payoff is a brighter, tidier smile that is visible after use.

The chain is direct: hydrogen peroxide or carbamide peroxide breaks down pigment molecules in the tooth, lightening its shade, while whitening toothpastes mainly remove surface stains with abrasives. Randomized trials and reviews show peroxide whitening changes tooth colour. Forum users also discuss DIY methods that have not been studied.
quick.how: Options range from over-the-counter strips and toothpastes to custom trays and in-office dentist treatments. Many people combine whitening with a cleaning, orthodontics or cosmetic dental work. Shade changes appear over days to weeks of use, depending on the product.
quick.risks: Tooth sensitivity is frequently reported, and strong peroxide can irritate or burn gums. Regulators limit peroxide strength in retail products, and over-abrasive products can damage tooth tissue.

angle.text: You whiten teeth with strips, pastes and dentist treatments, often alongside orthodontics, for a brighter and neater smile. Peroxide whitening breaks down tooth pigment, and the shade change is visible after use. Trials and reviews have measured colour change with peroxide products.

hair-dye-bleaching-hair.summary: Dyeing or bleaching scalp hair, brows, lashes or facial hair to change colour and contrast, cover grey and make sparse areas look fuller.

quick.overview:
Hair dyeing and bleaching change hair colour with chemical colourants or lighteners. Looksmaxxers use them on scalp hair, brows, lashes and facial hair to adjust contrast, cover grey, or make sparse eyebrows and beards look darker and fuller.

The chain is direct: permanent dyes use ammonia and peroxide to open the cuticle and form colour in the hair, and bleach oxidises melanin; semi-permanent and temporary dyes coat or sit under the cuticle and wash out. The chemistry is well documented, and the colour change is visible right after application.
quick.how: People apply boxed colour at home or have it done at a salon, choosing permanent, semi-permanent or temporary formulas depending on how long they want it to last. Brow and beard tints are usually done as shorter, targeted applications. Bleaching is often followed by toning and conditioning.
quick.risks: Allergy to PPD can cause itching, burning and sores, sometimes delayed, and can be severe. Peroxide bleaching can damage hair and skin. IARC lists some ingredients as mutagenic or carcinogenic, though overall evidence linking dye use to cancer is described as limited and inconsistent. The EU restricts many dye chemicals.

angle.text: You dye or bleach scalp hair, eyebrows, lashes or facial hair to change contrast, cover grey, or make sparse brows and beards look darker and fuller. The colour change is visible straight after application. It is a long-established cosmetic practice.

carrot-maxxing.summary: Eating large amounts of carrots and other carotenoid-rich foods to give skin a golden-orange tint without sun exposure.

quick.overview:
Carrot maxxing means eating lots of carrots or similar foods to give the skin a golden or orange tone without sun. The effect it relies on, carotenemia, is real and documented.

The chain is dietary: carotenoids from food accumulate in the outer skin layer and tint it. According to Wikipedia, colour typically appears after several weeks of high intake and fades over months after stopping. The medical literature on carotenemia consists of case descriptions and reviews focused on telling it apart from jaundice; no trials have tested it as a cosmetic method.
quick.how: People eat carotenoid-rich foods such as carrots, sweet potato and similar produce in large amounts daily, sometimes as juice. The tint builds gradually over weeks, often most visible on palms and soles and in the face, and it fades slowly once intake drops.
quick.risks: Carotenemia is generally described as benign, but it can mimic jaundice, and orange skin has been associated with conditions such as hypothyroidism and eating disorders. A report described amenorrhea in women with diet-induced carotenemia.

angle.text: You eat large amounts of carrots and other carotenoid-rich foods so carotenoids build up in the outer skin and give a golden glow without sun exposure. The tint builds over weeks. Carotenemia is a documented, benign condition described in the medical literature.

tyrosine-supplements-for-tanning.summary: Tyrosine pills or lotions taken on the theory that more of melanin's building block means a faster or deeper tan.

quick.overview:
L-tyrosine is a common amino acid and a building block of melanin, and some tanning products and supplement sellers suggest taking it orally or applying it topically to boost tanning. The appearance payoff people want is a faster or deeper tan.

The chain is biochemical: melanocytes convert tyrosine into melanin after UV exposure, so proponents reason that extra tyrosine supplies more raw material. Tyrosine's role in melanin is established biology; published supplement research has focused on neurotransmitters and performance under stress, and no human studies have tested it for tanning or skin colour.
quick.how: People take it as a supplement or use lotions containing it, usually alongside sun or sunbed sessions, as tyrosine does not replace UV in the tanning process.
quick.risks: Tyrosine is sold as a dietary supplement. The tanning it is paired with involves UV exposure, which is classified as a carcinogen and causes sunburn and skin ageing.

angle.text: You take tyrosine pills or apply lotions on the theory that more of melanin's building block means a faster or deeper tan. Tyrosine's role in melanin production is established biology. Human trials of it for tanning have not been published.

baby-oil-tanning.summary: Rubbing baby oil or tanning oil on before sunbathing for a deeper, glossier tan, a habit dating to the mid-twentieth century.

quick.overview:
Baby oil tanning means putting baby oil or a tanning oil on the skin before sunbathing, aiming for a faster, deeper and glossier tan. It was common in the 1950s and persists as a folk practice.

The chain people describe is that oil helps skin absorb or intensify the sun. UV light itself drives tanning by triggering melanin production, and the oil adds a glossy sheen rather than changing that process in any documented way. No studies have tested whether plain oil improves tanning. Oils began to be marketed in the 1920s, and SPF sunscreens appeared from 1962.
quick.how: People apply the oil in a thin layer before lying in the sun, sometimes reapplying during a session. It is typically used for beach or garden sunbathing, and the glossy finish is part of the appeal.
quick.risks: Oils without a sunscreen filter provide no UV protection, and the practice is associated with greater sunburn risk. Sunburn and UV-linked skin cancer are documented risks of sun exposure generally.

angle.text: You apply baby oil before sun exposure in the belief it speeds or deepens a tan and leaves a glossy finish, a habit dating to the mid-twentieth century. The oils typically contain no sunscreen filter. No studies have tested the claimed tanning benefit.

psoralen-puva-bergamot-oil-tanning.summary: A plant-derived light-sensitizer that makes skin tan more strongly under UVA; used medically as PUVA, but withdrawn from tanning products in 1996.

quick.overview:
Psoralens are light-sensitizing compounds found in plants such as figs, celery and citrus, including bergamot oil. With UVA light they darken skin, which is why tanning activators once used them to get a deeper tan faster. Doctors use them in PUVA therapy for conditions like psoriasis and vitiligo.

The chain is photochemical: psoralen enters the skin and, when hit by UVA, binds DNA and triggers damage responses and pigment production. Psoralen-based tanning activators were used in sun products until 1996, when they were banned after being found photocarcinogenic. Its cosmetic tanning effect is documented mainly from that older use.
quick.how: Historically, psoralen or bergamot oil was applied in tanning products before sun or UVA exposure. In medicine, PUVA is delivered under clinical supervision for skin conditions. Bergamot-oil use for tanning today is a fringe practice.
quick.risks: Documented harms include severe phototoxic burns and skin loss after sunbathing with psoralen products. Long-term PUVA is associated with higher skin cancer rates, including squamous cell carcinoma and melanoma, and psoralens are described as photocarcinogenic.

angle.text: Psoralen and bergamot oil were used in tanning products because they make skin respond more strongly to UVA, so users could darken faster. It is used medically as PUVA for skin conditions. Its tanning use was restricted in 1996 after phototoxic and photocarcinogenic findings.

nasal-tanning-spray.summary: Needle-free melanotan-style sprays sold online to darken skin without sun; unlicensed products with no published nasal-route study.

quick.overview:
Nasal tanning sprays are online products that claim to deliver melanotan-type peptides through the nose to darken skin without injections or sunbathing. They are not approved medicines.

The chain is hormonal: the active ingredients are synthetic analogues of alpha-MSH, such as melanotan II, which stimulates melanocytes to produce melanin. The peptides have been studied in injected form for pigment; whether a nasal route delivers meaningful amounts has no published study.
quick.how: People buy them online as a needle-free alternative to melanotan injections, usually alongside some sun exposure, and look for gradual darkening over weeks.
quick.risks: Regulators including the UK MHRA, Danish and Norwegian medicines agencies and the US FDA have warned against unlicensed melanotan products since 2007, noting possible impurities. Reported effects of melanotan II include flushing, nausea and mole darkening, and product contents are unverified.

angle.text: You buy nasal sprays as a needle-free way to get melanotan-style darkening without lying in the sun. The peptides involved mimic alpha-MSH, which stimulates melanin production, and have been studied in injected form. The nasal route for tanning has no published study.

sunbed-mt2-stack.summary: Pairing unlicensed melanotan II with tanning-bed sessions to build a deep tan in fewer sessions than either alone.

quick.overview:
The stack combines melanotan II, an unlicensed tanning peptide, with tanning bed sessions to darken skin faster and deeper. It circulates in looksmaxxing tanning discussions, with users reporting a deep tan in fewer sessions.

The chain is two-part: melanotan II mimics alpha-MSH to stimulate melanin production, while UV light triggers tanning directly, and proponents expect the two to add together. Each part is known to darken skin on its own; no studies have tested the combination.
quick.how: Users combine the peptide with regular sunbed sessions over several weeks, in the belief that melanin is already primed when UV arrives. Descriptions come from user reports rather than trials.
quick.risks: Melanotan II is unlicensed and regulators have warned against it since 2007. UV tanning devices are classified by IARC as Group 1 carcinogens and are linked to higher melanoma risk; reviews note melanoma reports in melanotan users may reflect extra UV exposure.

angle.text: You combine tanning-bed sessions with melanotan II to build a deep tan in fewer sessions than either alone: the peptide boosts melanin production and UV triggers pigment. Each part is known to darken skin by itself. The combination has not been trialled and rests on user reports.

primer-tan-base-tan.summary: Building a tan before a holiday so you arrive already bronzed; a UV-induced tan gives modest protection, around SPF 3.

quick.overview:
A primer or base tan is a tan built up before a trip or sun-heavy period, so you arrive already bronzed and, people hope, burn less. It is often gained through gradual sun exposure or tanning beds.

The chain is biological: UVB damages skin-cell DNA and triggers melanin production, which absorbs some UV. A UVB-induced tan has been described as giving modest protection, roughly SPF 3, meaning tanned skin tolerates up to about three times the exposure of pale skin. The tan itself arises from UV-induced DNA damage, and UVA darkening of existing melanin gives quick colour but no real protection.
quick.how: People expose skin in short, gradual sessions in the weeks before a trip, in the sun or on sunbeds, then continue sun care on holiday. The tan is visible within days of exposure.
quick.risks: UV exposure causes sunburn and is linked to skin cancer and ageing. Tanning devices are classified as carcinogenic to humans, and in two US surveys 58% of indoor tanners reported burns during sessions.

angle.text: You build a primer or base tan before a trip so you arrive already bronzed and, you hope, burn less. The tan is the visible result of UV triggering melanin production. The protection it gives has been measured as modest, around SPF 3.

red-light-tan-myth.summary: The idea that red or near-infrared light devices before sun or sunbed sessions prime skin to tan faster or deeper.

quick.overview:
Some looksmaxxing and skincare posters say that exposing skin to red or near-infrared light from LED panels or masks before sun or sunbed sessions prepares it to tan faster or deeper. The appearance payoff wanted is a quicker, deeper tan.

The chain proponents suggest is that red light stimulates skin cells in a way that boosts pigment response. Red light therapy (photobiomodulation) has been studied mainly for wound healing and pain, and no published study tests it as a tanning primer. Natural tanning is described as driven by UV acting on melanocytes.
quick.how: Users run a red-light panel or mask over the skin for a session before UV exposure, often as part of a wider skincare routine. Descriptions come from informal reasoning on forums.
quick.risks: Red light devices are cleared by the FDA for some uses, and some users report mild irritation or pain; long-term skin effects are described as not known. Tanning with UV carries documented risks, including sunburn and increased skin cancer risk.

angle.text: Some posters say red-light devices used before sun or bed sessions prime skin to tan more readily. The idea is that red light stimulates skin cells and boosts pigment response. Red light therapy has been studied for wound healing and pain, and no published study tests it for tanning.

tan-lines-meta.summary: Deliberately showing, hiding or evening out tan lines for a seamless bronze look or a style detail.

quick.overview:
Tan lines are the contrast between skin exposed to sun and skin covered by clothing or swimwear. Some people manage them for an even, seamless bronze, while others keep them on display as a style detail. The result is visible immediately.

The chain is mechanical: tanning occurs when melanocytes make melanin in response to UV, and covered skin gets none, so it stays lighter. People adjust clothing and positioning, or use sunless tanners and bronzers, to control where colour shows. Tan-through swimwear was introduced in 1969, and no clinical studies on tan line management exist.
quick.how: People choose swimwear, straps and positioning to control where sun reaches, wear tan-through fabrics, or even out colour afterward with sunless tanner or bronzer. Others leave lines intentionally for effect.
quick.risks: Added UV exposure to even a tan raises the risk of sunburn, premature ageing and skin cancer. Sunless products avoid UV but can streak or look orange if applied unevenly, and bronzers can rub off on clothing.

angle.text: You manage tan lines on purpose, either evening them out for a seamless bronze look or showing them off as a style detail. Clothing, positioning or sunless products control where colour shows, and the result is visible immediately. It is a presentation choice.

vitamin-d-uvb-for-tan.summary: Sun or sunbed UVB exposure that serves two goals at once: vitamin D production and a tan.

quick.overview:
UVB radiation in sunlight both stimulates new melanin, which gives a tan, and drives vitamin D production in skin. Some people cite vitamin D as a reason for sun or sunbed exposure that also gives them colour, so the two goals are often pursued together.

The chain is shared: UVB converts a skin precursor into vitamin D3, and the same UVB band prompts melanocytes to make new melanin, producing a tan that appears two to three days later. Melanin absorbs UV and reduces UVB-driven vitamin D synthesis, which is why darker skin makes less for the same exposure. Small trials have measured vitamin D after sunbed or UVB exposure.
quick.how: People get UVB through sun exposure or sunbeds, and the tan appears a few days after a session. Vitamin D can also come from diet and supplements, and health bodies publish intake guidance that does not depend on tanning.
quick.risks: Excess UV is linked to sunburn, skin ageing, DNA damage and skin cancer.

angle.text: Some people frame UVB sun exposure as serving two goals at once: vitamin D production and a tan. UVB drives both, with new melanin showing as colour a few days after exposure. Vitamin D can also come from diet or supplements.

tanning-oil.summary: Oils applied while sunbathing to deepen colour and give a glossy bronzed finish; sunless DHA oils give colour without UV.

quick.overview:
Tanning oils are cosmetic oils applied to skin in the sun to deepen colour and give a glossy bronzed finish. Jean Patou's 1927 product is described as the first, and baby oil was common in the 1950s.

The chain is cosmetic: sun-exposure oils do not themselves darken skin, since tanning comes from UV acting on melanocytes, but they add sheen to the result. A newer category blends oils with DHA, which colours the dead outer skin layer through a browning reaction without UV. No clinical trials of tanning oils for appearance were found.
quick.how: People apply the oil before or during sunbathing, or choose a DHA-based oil to build colour without sun. Many pair it with sun exposure for a glossy finish.
quick.risks: Sunburn is the most common UV hazard, and excess exposure raises skin cancer risk. Oils with low or no SPF offer little protection, and DHA colour does not protect from UV.

angle.text: You apply tanning oil while sunbathing to deepen colour and give skin a glossy bronzed finish. The tan comes from sun exposure, and oils have been used for this since the 1920s. Sunless DHA oils give colour without UV.

tanning-drops-isle-of-paradise-style.summary: Self-tan concentrate drops mixed into your moisturiser so you can choose how deep and gradual your colour builds.

quick.overview:
Tanning drops are concentrated self-tanning products added to your own lotion or skincare so colour deepens with the amount used. Isle of Paradise is one brand associated with the format. The appeal is a custom-shade glow without sun.

The chain is chemical: self-tanners generally rely on DHA, which reacts with amino acids in the dead outer layer of skin in a Maillard-type browning reaction, with no UV or melanin involved. The colour appears within hours and builds over days. No clinical studies of the format were found.
quick.how: People mix a few drops into their usual moisturiser, serum or body lotion, adding more for a deeper result, and apply it as they would normally. Colour builds gradually with repeated use.
quick.risks: DHA colour fades over roughly 3 to 10 days, and misapplication can produce orange or splotchy results. Skin may be more UV-susceptible for about 24 hours after DHA use, and contact dermatitis is reported.

angle.text: You mix self-tan drops into your moisturiser to choose how deep and how gradual a tan looks, building colour over days. DHA colours the outer skin layer without UV. The colour change is visible within hours.

tanning-wipes-towelettes.summary: Pre-soaked self-tan wipes for a quick, portable way to add temporary bronzed colour without a mitt or bottle.

quick.overview:
Tanning wipes are pre-moistened cloths impregnated with a self-tanning or bronzing composition, such as DHA, that you wipe over the skin. The payoff is quick, portable bronzed colour without a bottle or mitt.

The chain is the same as other self-tanners: DHA reacts with the dead outer skin layer to give colour without UV, and the colour shows as it develops. A patent filing describes the concept of tissue impregnated with tanning lotion, oil or bronzing agent; no clinical studies of the category were found.
quick.how: People wipe the cloth over face and body in even strokes, often for travel or touch-ups. Colour develops over hours and fades in about 3 to 10 days.
quick.risks: Uneven wiping can cause streaking or orange colour, and DHA is not approved around eyes, lips or mucous membranes. Bronzers may rub off on clothing.

angle.text: You reach for tanning wipes for a quick, portable way to add bronzed colour without a mitt or bottle. DHA or bronzer tints the skin, and the colour shows as it develops. It is temporary and fades within days.
